content: KeePass Password Safe is intended to help users manage many passwords without repeatedly reusing or memorizing them. It should store passwords, usernames, email accounts, URLs, and related notes in an encrypted database protected by a master credential. Users also need a practical way to organize and use the stored entries while keeping the database portable between computers.

People often need that when they use a desktop at work and a laptop at home, or when they switch between different office computers and want the same passwords available everywhere. Success means they can move or open the same database on another machine without losing data, and it works reliably without having to rebuild anything manually. Ideally they can carry it on a USB stick or sync it in a way that still keeps it secure and intact.

It should remain a single self-contained file that can be copied or moved as-is to another computer and opened there with the master credential. Nothing in the file should depend on that specific machine, so users don’t have to export and re-import entries or recreate the database. The main expectation is that portability doesn’t weaken the encryption or change how the data is organized.

The main users are individual people who have a lot of accounts to manage, especially employees or anyone handling work and personal logins across many sites and systems. Day to day, they need to quickly find an entry, copy the username or password when needed, and keep notes like URLs or extra account details together in one place. They also need to organize entries so the list doesn’t become unmanageable as it grows.

A successful experience means they can search or browse to the right entry very quickly, even if there are hundreds or thousands of records, and then copy out what they need without much friction. It should still feel manageable to organize things into groups or folders so people aren’t scrolling through one giant list. What we want to avoid is the database becoming slow, hard to navigate, or so cluttered that users start losing confidence in whether they can find the right credential when they need it.

I’d expect the structure to stay simple and predictable, with folders or groups used mainly for human-friendly organization rather than anything too complex. Deep nesting can become hard to browse, so I’d prefer it to be limited or at least not encouraged too heavily, but I don’t know that we have a firm maximum in mind yet. Shared entries across multiple groups sound convenient, but I’d want to verify whether that adds too much complexity; the main goal is that users can keep the database easy to understand and maintain over time.

My expectation is that it should behave like one master entry, so if something changes, it stays linked everywhere and users don’t have to update multiple copies by hand. Having separate copies in different groups would be risky because people could end up with conflicting passwords or notes. If we support multiple appearances, they should just be different views of the same underlying record unless there’s a very specific reason not to.

Users should be able to create, edit, and delete entries as a normal part of managing their passwords. If something gets deleted by mistake, it would be very helpful to have some kind of restore or undo capability, at least for recent changes, because losing a credential record can be disruptive. I’m not sure yet whether that should be a full recycle bin or just a short-term undo, but some recovery option would be valuable.

There should be a straightforward import path from whatever source users already have, like another password manager or a file export, so they can get started without retyping everything. Ideally the process maps common fields like title, username, password, URL, and notes into the new database cleanly and tells the user if anything couldn’t be brought over. After import, the database should be immediately usable, with the user able to organize and verify the entries before relying on it day to day.

Both. Some users will start fresh, and others will be migrating from an old tool or an export file, so we need to support either path. It would also be helpful if they could import into an existing database later, not only during the first setup.

It should feel like a normal maintenance task, not a special project. The user should be able to open the existing database, choose an import source, review what’s coming in, and then merge it in with the current entries without losing their existing organization. If there are conflicts or duplicates, the system should point them out clearly so they can decide what to keep.

For the first release, the essential capabilities are secure encrypted storage, a master credential to open the database, basic creation and editing of entries, simple grouping or folder organization, and import so people can actually get their passwords in there. Later versions can add more advanced conveniences like richer search, more automation, syncing, or more elaborate recovery and sharing features. The first version really just needs to be safe, usable, and portable.

If the master credential is entered incorrectly, the system should simply refuse access and make it clear that the unlock failed, but I would not expect any kind of account recovery built into the first release. If it’s forgotten, that’s a serious problem because the database is encrypted, so I’d expect the product to be honest about that rather than pretending recovery is possible. Changing the master credential later should be supported, but only after the user is already unlocked and can deliberately update it.

Day to day, users should open the local database, unlock it with the master credential, look up or edit the entries they need, and then lock it again when they’re done. It should stay simple enough that people can actually use it regularly, but the data should remain encrypted whenever it’s not actively in use. I’d also expect the file to be something they can keep on their own machine or carry with them, rather than being forced into an always-online setup.

It should not be stored in plain text in local files, and we should avoid keeping it around longer than necessary in memory. Some temporary exposure during unlock is probably unavoidable if the application needs to use it to access the database, but it should be minimized as much as practical. From the user’s point of view, the expectation is that the product protects the credential as much as it reasonably can while still staying usable.

Yes, I’d want an automatic lock after a period of inactivity so a user doesn’t leave an unlocked database sitting open all day by accident. I’m not sure what exact timeout is right, but it should be configurable because different people will have different comfort levels and work habits. When it locks, the sensitive material should be cleared as much as the application can manage.

When it locks, the sensitive material on screen should disappear and any temporary session data should be cleared out, especially anything tied to the master credential or decrypted entry contents. I wouldn’t want exceptions for the core secrets, because that weakens the point of locking. The only thing that might reasonably remain is non-sensitive structure or navigation state, if that helps the user return to where they were without exposing the data itself.

I’d expect a mixed audience, including people who are not very technical and may be coming from spreadsheets, browser-saved passwords, or even paper notes. That suggests the product should keep the language plain, avoid jargon, and make the first-time experience very guided without being overwhelming. It should feel approachable, with clear labels and help that explains the basics in everyday terms.

They’d mostly use it when they need to log into a website or software account, add a new password after creating an account, update an existing entry when credentials change, or look up notes tied to an account. They would typically open the app directly on their computer, unlock the database, and then copy or read the needed details from the entry they’re working with. In some cases they’d probably keep the database file on removable media or in a synced location so they can use it on more than one machine.

It mostly depends on how many accounts they use and whether they keep getting prompted to sign in during the day, so some people may open it just once or twice while others will unlock it many times. If the auto-lock is too aggressive, they’ll end up re-entering the master credential more often, so there has to be a balance between convenience and security. I wouldn’t expect a hard limit on how often they can unlock it, just normal practical use without the app getting in the way.

I’d want the product to make it easy to create backups and restore from them, because people will absolutely need a fallback if a file gets lost or corrupted. It should support keeping copies wherever the user chooses, like local disks, removable media, or other storage they trust, but the app itself doesn’t need to manage a whole backup system. Restoring from an older copy should be straightforward, since that’s a practical recovery scenario.

It should help them stop reusing the same password across sites, because that’s one of the biggest risks they’re trying to avoid. It also needs to protect the master credential very well, since that becomes the single key to everything stored in the database. Ideally it should encourage strong, unique passwords without making the user feel like they have to memorize them all.

I’d expect the product to avoid making silent guesses in those cases. If an imported entry clearly conflicts with an existing one, the safest behavior is to let the user review it and decide which version to keep, or whether to merge the details. Automatic replacement could be okay only when the user has explicitly chosen that behavior for the import.

It should preserve as much information as possible instead of dropping those fields. If a field doesn’t map cleanly, the user should be able to store it in a notes area or a custom field, and missing values should just remain empty rather than causing the import to fail. The important thing is that the import remains usable and the user can see what came in and what didn’t fit neatly.

They should be able to compare the main pieces of the entry side by side, like the username, password, URL, title, notes, and any custom fields that were carried over. It would also be helpful if they can edit the incoming data during review before saving it, so they can merge the useful parts instead of choosing only one version. The goal is to make the decision clear without forcing them to reopen and fix things afterward.

Yes, the password field should be treated with extra care, so it shouldn’t just sit there fully exposed by default. It can be shown on demand or masked until the user chooses to reveal it, while still allowing them to compare it when necessary. Other sensitive fields like notes might also deserve careful handling, but the password is the main one I’d call out.

I’d say it should mostly be controlled by the field type and by an explicit user action. Passwords should stay masked by default and only be revealed if the user deliberately asks for it, while notes or similar fields could probably be shown if the user is already reviewing that record. I wouldn’t want the product to block them entirely, just keep the reveal under user control.

It should still be self-contained and open the same way on another computer as long as the user has the master credential. I wouldn’t expect the file format or encryption to change just because it was copied elsewhere, and it shouldn’t depend on being tied to one machine. The only real restriction should be that the database stays protected until it’s unlocked with the proper credential.

In practice, I’d expect there to be some kind of undo for accidental deletion at least immediately after the action, because that’s the most common mistake. Beyond that, whether deleted entries are kept recoverable for a longer time or permanently removed is something I’d want the product team to decide, because it depends on how much safety versus simplicity we want. I don’t think ordinary users should be able to restore things forever once they’ve been deliberately purged.

It should fail safely and leave the database untouched and still locked. The user should get a clear message that the unlock didn’t succeed, whether that was because the master credential was wrong or because the process was interrupted. I wouldn’t want any partial state saved or any chance of corruption from that.

A restored copy should be verifiable and openable as long as it’s still a valid encrypted database, regardless of which device it’s on. If the backup is older, the product should probably warn the user that some entries may be out of date compared with their current data, but it shouldn’t block opening it. If the backup looks incomplete or damaged, then it should clearly tell the user before they try to rely on it.

I’d expect it to look for basic integrity problems, like failing to decrypt properly, missing required structure in the database, or entries that can’t be read back cleanly. If those checks fail, the warning should say that the backup may be incomplete, corrupted, or not fully restorable, and that the user should not rely on it as their only copy. It should be clear enough that they know they may need to go back to another backup or their original database.

Yes, if the backup is clearly older than another available copy and it’s missing known newer data, the warning should be stronger. I’d want it to make plain that opening it could mean looking at stale information and that the user may overwrite more recent changes if they’re not careful. But it should still allow the file to open, because sometimes an older backup is exactly what the user needs.

Yes, I’d treat it as safest if nothing is exposed until the unlock is fully successful. If the process stops before it finishes, it should just abandon the attempt and leave the database locked, with no partial data shown or written back. If any internal work has started, that should still be temporary and rolled back cleanly so the user sees no change except that the unlock didn’t complete.

I’d expect existing users to be able to keep opening older databases for some period, so they aren’t forced into a migration right away. If an upgrade to the file format is needed, it should probably be a deliberate action with a clear warning that the new format may not be readable by older versions. Automatic upgrade on open feels risky unless we’re very sure there’s a safe fallback or a backup is created first.

I’d prefer the original older file be preserved as a backup by default, at least until the user has confirmed the new version works for them. Replacing it in place feels too risky because if something goes wrong, they could lose the last known good copy. Ideally the product would make the new file alongside the old one, or clearly offer both choices and explain the tradeoff.

If the user is just opening the older file in a newer version and no upgrade is required, I’d keep using the original file as the active source so there’s no duplication or confusion. If the newer version needs a format upgrade, then it should create a separate upgraded copy and leave the original untouched, because that gives the user a safe rollback path if they later go back to an earlier version. The main rule should be that we don’t silently trap them in a format their old version can’t read.

I’d keep the wording simple and familiar, using terms like master password, database, entry, group, and search rather than technical storage or encryption language. For first-time setup, the helper text should explain in plain words that the master password unlocks everything and cannot be recovered if forgotten. On everyday screens, labels should be short and obvious, with optional extra hints for things like saving, copying passwords, or adding notes so both new and experienced users can work quickly.

It should say exactly what happened in plain language, like that the item is locked, the database isn’t open, or the clipboard copy failed. If it can’t be done right away, I’d want a brief message that explains whether the user needs to unlock the database, retry, or check permissions. The important part is that it doesn’t just fail silently, because that would be confusing.

I’d leave the exact wording undecided for now. I think we have enough direction on the style and meaning, but the final labels should probably be refined later with actual UI drafts so they read naturally in context.

It should depend on the cause of the failure. If the database is locked, the app should ask the user to unlock it; if it’s a temporary problem like clipboard access or a brief save failure, it should offer retry; and if it’s a permission or state issue that the user can’t resolve immediately, it should explain what needs to change first.

It should prompt the user to enter the master credential to unlock the database, and then continue the action they were trying to perform. If the user is already in the middle of something that can’t be resumed cleanly, it can just return them to the unlocked database without retrying automatically. If the file itself can’t be opened or is missing, then it shouldn’t ask to unlock at all, because that’s a different problem.
